label: Impulse!
rationale: This is the ballad record of Coltrane's Classic Quartet - the only album he made with a singer as co-leader, and the one that fixed Johnny Hartman in the canon: 'Hartman is the only vocalist with whom the saxophonist recorded as a leader' [S1] (obs). It has become a classic ballad jazz album, and its readings of 'Lush Life', 'My One and Only Love' and 'They Say It's Wonderful' are called definitive [S1] (obs). Consensus across independent listing traditions: Wikipedia's review box records AllMusic 5/5, the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 5/5, The Encyclopedia of Popular Music 4/5 and The Penguin Guide to Jazz 3.5/5 - US guides emphatic, Penguin notably cooler; Scott Yanow's AllMusic review calls it 'essential for all jazz collections', and it was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2013 [S1] (obs). Session gravity is high: one date, March 7, 1963, with the working quartet at its peak - Coltrane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, Elvin Jones - all six tunes cut in single takes except 'You Are Too Beautiful', which needed two because Elvin Jones dropped a stick [S1,S3] (obs). Lineage: the canon holds the quartet's A Love Supreme (1964) and Duke Ellington & John Coltrane (1963); this is the same band on the other side of its register, and Kurt Elling's 2009 Dedicated to You is a full-album tribute to it [S1] (obs). It still plays: plainly a record a curious listener can be sent to cold - a singer and a saxophone, unhurried, thirty-one minutes [S2] (inf). Style note: AllMusic files it under Jazz/Vocal with styles Standards, Vocal Jazz, Torch Songs - no genre bucket - so the canon code is a judgment call; filed post-bop to match the canon's filing of the 1963 Coltrane Impulse! date Duke Ellington & John Coltrane, and the council may prefer hard-bop (the canon's code for its other vocal-with-jazz-group record, Sarah Vaughan with Clifford Brown, 1954) - John rules.

personnel.name: John Coltrane
personnel.notes: Co-leader. Later overdubbed additional obbligato saxophone phrases behind the vocal on 'My One and Only Love', 'Lush Life' and 'You Are Too Beautiful'; a new master with added echo replaced the original master after first release [S1].

personnel.name: Johnny Hartman
personnel.notes: The only vocalist Coltrane recorded with as a leader [S1]. Per Hartman, every song was cut in one take except 'You Are Too Beautiful', which took two [S1].

tracks.title: You Are Too Beautiful
tracks.notes: Took two takes at the session; the released take is the one recorded after Elvin Jones dropped a drumstick [S1].

personnel_record.notes: Single session, March 7, 1963, Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, NJ - all six tracks from one date [S1,S3,S5]. Engineer/producer confirmed by three independent sources (MusicBrainz per-track credits, Qobuz, the library catalogue's 'original sessions produced by Bob Thiele') [S3,S4,S5]. Track order and side assignment follow the LP (side one: 1-3; side two: 4-6) [S1]. Barry Kernfeld's 2005 tape review documented complete alternate takes of all six songs, unreleased pending ownership between the Coltrane family and Universal Music; no reissue additions are listed here [S1].

ballot.album: John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman — John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman (1963)
ballot.case_for: The album is Hartman’s defining recording and Coltrane’s only album with a vocalist as leader, pairing him with the Classic Quartet for celebrated readings of standards including “Lush Life” [S1, S3]. Its landmark standing is supported by high ratings from AllMusic and the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide, Grammy Hall of Fame induction, and Yanow’s “essential for all jazz collections” assessment [S1]. The focused, accessible 31-minute session also extends the picture of the quartet already represented in the canon, showing its lyrical ballad register [S1, S2, S3].
ballot.case_against: This is a songbook ballad date rather than a major step in post-bop’s harmonic or rhythmic development: Coltrane mainly accompanies Hartman and offers concise ballad statements, making it less central to the tradition’s innovations than records such as A Love Supreme. Critical consensus is strong but not uniform: Penguin’s 3.5/5 is cooler than the top ratings cited from other guides [S1].
ballot.disagreement: Both references judge the album consensus_core, but differ on priority: one rates it strong because the canon is not visibly incomplete without it, while the other calls it must_have as an indispensable cornerstone of vocal-tenor jazz.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John treat this as a consensus-core, strong-priority candidate that adds an essential lyrical dimension to the Classic Quartet’s story.
